name: Azure Blob Storage
summary: Azure’s object storage, with three blob types and an optional real directory tree for analytics.
intro: Blob Storage nests data three levels deep: a storage account holds containers, and containers hold blobs. Unlike most object stores, a blob has one of three types, fixed at creation. Block blobs are ordinary files, uploaded as up to 50,000 blocks and committed in one step, for a maximum of about 190.7 TiB. Append blobs only grow at the end, which suits logs. Page blobs are made of 512-byte pages you can overwrite in place, up to 8 TiB, and they are what Azure VM disks are built on.

Block blobs sit in an access tier: hot, cool, cold or archive. Cool and cold bill for at least 30 and 90 days. Archive is offline: it bills for at least 180 days, and a blob must be rehydrated before you can read it, which can take up to 15 hours. Turning on the hierarchical namespace (Azure Data Lake Storage) adds real directories, so renaming or deleting a folder updates one entry instead of millions of blobs. Spark and Hive jobs that rename their output depend on this.
strengths: Append and page blobs cover logs and random writes that plain objects can’t
Four tiers plus lifecycle rules, and a smart tier that moves blobs between hot, cool and cold by usage
Hierarchical namespace gives atomic directory renames for analytics engines
Also reachable over NFS 3.0 and SFTP when enabled on the account
limits: No S3 API: tools need Azure’s own REST API or SDKs
Archived blobs take up to 15 hours to rehydrate, and the archive tier only works with LRS, GRS or RA-GRS redundancy, not zone-redundant accounts
Early deletion fees apply if you delete or re-tier a blob before the tier’s minimum days
The hierarchical namespace can’t be turned off once enabled, and some Blob features don’t support it

snippet.title: Create an account and container, upload to cool, then archive
source: az storage account create --name acmemedia --resource-group media-rg \
az storage container create --account-name acmemedia --name photos --auth-mode login
az storage blob upload --account-name acmemedia --container-name photos \
# archive is offline: reading it later needs a rehydrate of up to 15 hours
az storage blob set-tier --account-name acmemedia --container-name photos \

story: Microsoft announced Windows Azure on 27 October 2008 at its Professional Developers Conference, where chief software architect Ray Ozzie described it as “the bedrock, underneath all of Microsoft’s service offerings”. Its storage service, Windows Azure Storage, went into production that November with three abstractions: Blobs for files, Tables for structured data and Queues for messages. The platform became commercially available on 1 February 2010.

Brad Calder and a large Microsoft team described the design at SOSP in 2011. Where S3 was then eventually consistent, Azure promised strong consistency, because enterprise customers moving line-of-business applications to the cloud asked for it. The system grew out of Cosmos, Bing’s internal storage system, which Azure extended into an append-only “stream layer”. Microsoft used it heavily itself: one Bing pipeline kept around 350 TB of public Facebook and Twitter posts in it to make them searchable within 15 seconds.
Later additions turned it into an archive and a data lake: an offline Archive tier in 2017, a hierarchical namespace for analytics (Data Lake Storage Gen2) in 2019, and automatic tiering in 2026.

choices.why: Customers wanted a read to see the latest write, and conditional updates for optimistic concurrency. Azure put a strongly consistent partition layer on top of a simple replicated layer to get both availability and consistency within a cluster.
Never overwriting committed data “greatly simplified the replication protocol”, made snapshots almost free and eased erasure coding. The price is a garbage collector that reclaims dead space.

choices.choice: Three blob types instead of one
choices.why: Page blobs, with 512-byte pages you can overwrite in place, let virtual machine disks live in blob storage; append blobs fit logs; block blobs cover ordinary files.
On a flat namespace, renaming a folder of 5,000 blobs took 10,000 REST calls and could fail halfway. Data Lake Storage Gen2 made such renames a single atomic operation for Hadoop and Spark.

timeline.text: Windows Azure announced at PDC in October; storage enters production in November
Commercially available on 1 February, with Blobs, Tables and Queues
SOSP paper describes Windows Azure Storage and its strong consistency
Archive tier generally available at $0.002 per GB-month (December)
Data Lake Storage Gen2 adds a hierarchical namespace; GA on 7 February
Smart tier moves blobs between hot, cool and cold automatically (April)
